Document in the team wiki that only stewards should certify assets, and review the tags once a year
Restrict the ASSIGN permission on the `system.certification_status` governed tag to the stewards group
Rename the working-copy tables with a `_draft` suffix so that engineers recognise them as unapproved

stem: A travel agent is built on LangGraph, and the framework's own checkpointer already persists the graph state of each chat, so a chat resumes after a restart. Travelers now complain that a seat preference stated in one chat is unknown in the next chat. What should the team add?

choices.text: Append a growing list of the travelers' stated preferences to the shared system prompt used by the chats
Add agent memory for durable preferences recalled by semantic search, and keep the checkpointer for in-chat state
Replace the checkpointer's persisted graph state with agent memory so the agent keeps one store for both needs
Move the checkpointer state into an agent session store, since a session carries the traveler's state into later chats

stem: A planning agent crashes midway through a long conversation and restarts. Its memory store still holds the user's stable preferences, but after the restart the agent has lost the tool calls and intermediate results it had gathered in this conversation. Which memory strategy closes the gap?

choices.text: Persist the interaction's working state in an agent session and read it at the start of each turn so the conversation resumes
Run the memory pipeline more often so every tool result becomes a long-term memory entry the moment it is produced
Remove the memory store and keep all preferences in the conversation, so that one component holds all state
Store the intermediate results as embeddings in the memory store and rely on semantic search to rebuild the plan order

stem: A travel agent already keeps each chat in a session store. The team wants it to act on the following needs. Which TWO needs require long-term memory rather than session history? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Reusing the departure city the user typed a minute ago while refining the same search
Keeping the result of the flight search that was run two turns ago in the same conversation
Showing the three most recent messages again after the user scrolls back up in the open chat
Remembering that this traveler always wants an aisle seat and a vegetarian meal when booking in any later trip
Recalling that last spring the traveler rejected a particular airline because of a baggage dispute

stem: A team lead reads the Databricks memory research mapping and asks which component plays which role. Which statement matches how the docs map the session store, the memory store and the memory pipeline?

choices.text: Both stores hold episodic memory, and the pipeline fine-tunes the model on them during an offline step so that sessions are no longer needed
The session store holds derived memory, the memory store holds the raw record, and the pipeline replays that record into every new prompt
The session store holds episodic memory, the raw record of each session; the memory store holds derived memory; the pipeline distills the first into the second
The session store holds derived memory, the memory store holds episodic memory, and the pipeline copies the episodic records back into sessions

stem: A research agent works on one very long task in a single conversation. Its trace shows the context filling up with early tool outputs, and a teammate proposes adding a cross-user long-term memory store to fix it. Why is that the wrong memory strategy, and what fits better?

choices.text: Long-term memory is only for system prompts, so the earlier tool outputs should be moved into the system prompt
The problem is in-interaction state growth, so trim or compact the session's context and keep large results outside the window
Long-term memory cannot be searched semantically, so the agent should use keyword lookups of its earlier tool outputs instead
Memory stores are deleted whenever a session ends, so nothing could be recalled for the remainder of the task

stem: A compliance team wants a complete record of every interaction an assistant had, available for replay, and also wants the assistant to personalize answers from what it learned about each customer. Which store layout matches these two information needs?

choices.text: Keep the full replayable records in the session store and the distilled customer facts in the memory store, fed by a memory pipeline
Keep replayable records in the memory store and distilled facts in the system prompt, rewritten whenever a customer returns
Keep both needs in the session store, and let the agent search old transcripts each time it personalizes an answer
Keep both needs in one memory store, since distilled facts and replayable records have the same scope

stem: An agent runs a multi-day vendor onboarding workflow across many job runs. It tracks which of the checklist steps are done in a scratchpad it writes into its own context. After a restart and after a compaction, the checklist is gone and finished steps are repeated. What should the team change?

choices.text: Increase the maximum output length so the scratchpad can hold the full checklist history in each response
Ask the model to keep a running summary of the checklist at the end of every reply so compaction preserves it
Write the steps to a longer scratchpad in the system prompt so that the checklist is always at the top of the window
Store task and step status in a Delta table that the agent reads and updates, and load only the rows it needs each step

stem: A math tutoring agent solves a problem in one turn. It writes a three-line plan, computes two intermediate values, and then answers in the same turn. Nothing is needed after the turn ends. Which approach to the intermediate state is best?

choices.text: Create a Delta state table with a row per intermediate value so the work is auditable by future runs
Write the values to a Lakebase table and read them back at the start of the next unrelated conversation
Keep the plan and values in an in-context scratchpad for the turn because nothing needs to outlive it
Save the plan to the agent memory store as a durable fact so the tutor can reuse it for other students

stem: Several agents work in parallel on one claims case: an intake agent, a document agent and a fraud agent. They each need to see which sub-tasks others finished, and an auditor must later query who did what and when. Which TWO designs meet these needs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Record each agent's actions as rows with timestamps and agent ids in that same Delta table so auditors can query them with SQL
Hold sub-task status only in the memory store as semantically searchable facts about the case
Have each agent keep its own scratchpad and exchange summaries of it by pasting them into the next agent's prompt
Rely on the orchestrator's context window to hold all sub-task status and reconstruct the audit trail from its trace
Store sub-task state in a shared Delta table keyed by case and sub-task, which every agent reads and updates

stem: A coding agent keeps appending a note to its scratchpad after every tool call. By step forty, the trace shows the scratchpad filling the window with notes about steps that finished long ago, and the agent starts misreading the current step. What change best fits?

choices.text: Tell the agent to write shorter notes from now on, and keep all of them in the scratchpad
Duplicate the scratchpad into the system prompt so that the current step is read twice
Reformat the notes in a different markup style so that the important ones are marked as high priority in the window
Move the finished steps into a Delta state table and keep in the window only the active step and the notes it needs

stem: A data-quality agent compares thousands of rows across tables and must track a counter, a list of failed checks and the last row processed. Runs can be interrupted and resumed hours later by a different worker. Which approach is the most reliable?

choices.text: Ask the model to track the counter and failed checks in its scratchpad and recompute them whenever the run resumes
Store the counter, failed checks and last processed position in a Delta state table and have each resumed run read them before continuing
Print the counter and failed checks into the final answer so the next worker can copy them from the previous message
Put the failed-check list in the memory store as a semantically searchable fact and fetch it by similarity when the run resumes

stem: A billing agent stores each customer's facts as rows in Lakebase Postgres. A user asks, "What is my current plan tier?" The tier is a single column on the customer row identified by the authenticated customer id. Which retrieval approach fits?

choices.text: Run a hybrid keyword and similarity search over the whole table and take the top-ranked row
A structured SQL query that filters the row by customer id and selects the tier column
Embed all customer rows into an index and run a similarity search with the question text
Ask the model to guess the tier from the previous conversation summary and verify it later

stem: A wellness agent stores free-text notes from earlier chats. A user now says, "Remember that thing we talked about when I was stressed about my sister's wedding?" No note contains the words "stressed" or "wedding"; they say "anxious about family event." Which retrieval approach should the agent use over the stored notes?

choices.text: A structured query ordered by note timestamp, returning the latest note
A SQL equality filter on the word "wedding" in the notes column
A SQL LIKE pattern for "stressed" so the agent can match notes containing the same word
Semantic search over embeddings of the notes, ranked by meaning

stem: An account agent can look up memory two ways: a structured SQL query on Lakebase tables, or semantic search over note text. Which TWO lookups should use the structured query? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Count how many support cases for this account were closed during the current quarter
Find notes that resemble how an unhappy customer described a recurring outage in their own words
Recall earlier chats where the user hinted at being worried about budget without stating a number
Surface notes semantically close to a vague phrase such as "the thing about my shipment"
Return the account's current preferred_language value stored as a column on the customer row

stem: An agent keeps memory about product orders, with notes such as "replacement for XK-9921-B shipped late". When a user asks about order "XK-9921-B", pure embedding search ranks notes about other products with similar-sounding descriptions above the exact identifier match. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Remove identifiers from the notes before embedding so the search focuses on meaning only
Increase the embedding dimension of the notes so identifiers become more distinct in vector space
Use hybrid keyword-similarity search so exact identifier matches are scored alongside semantic matches
Lower the number of results returned to one so the first similarity hit is always the right one

stem: A shared agent stores memories for many customers. A semantic search for "my last complaint" returns a close match that belongs to a different customer, and the trace shows the other customer's note in the prompt. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Raise the similarity threshold so that only near-identical notes are returned for any query
Switch to a larger embedding model so that notes from different customers become easier to tell apart by meaning
Apply a customer id filter as a predicate on the search, so only that customer's notes are candidates
Add instructions to the system prompt telling the model to ignore notes that mention other customers

stem: A team runs three memory-injection configurations through the same evaluation dataset and judges, five MLflow runs each, and records correctness: config A mean 0.84 (range 0.62 to 0.95), config B mean 0.81 (range 0.78 to 0.84), config C mean 0.70 (range 0.69 to 0.71). Which configuration is the most stable choice for production?

choices.text: Config C, because its range is the narrowest and consistency matters more than quality
Config A, because it reached the highest single score and can be tuned to match it every time
Config A, because mean correctness is the only quantity that matters when comparing runs
Config B, because its results stay in a narrow range at a high level across repeated runs

stem: A team evaluates a memory-enabled agent with MLflow 3 on 80 single-turn questions, each answerable from the question text alone, once with memory injection off and once on. Correctness is 0.83 in both runs, and the team concludes that memory adds nothing. What is wrong with this conclusion and what is the fix?

choices.text: Memory should be judged on latency only, so drop the quality scorers and compare the duration of the traces for both runs
The dataset never needs earlier-conversation facts, so add rows that depend on prior chats, with expectations, and rerun both configurations
The judge is too lenient, so replace correctness with a stricter groundedness judge and score the same single-turn questions again
Two runs are too few, so repeat each configuration ten times and base the decision on the larger mean of the same dataset

stem: Two memory configurations score the same mean correctness in MLflow. Config X injects a short summary of the user's history; config Y injects the five most recent raw transcript snippets. The team must decide which to ship and can inspect the evaluation traces. Which evidence best breaks the tie?

choices.text: Compare per-trace judge feedback on the lowest-scoring rows and the tokens each configuration put into the context
Pick config Y because longer injected text always indicates a richer memory and therefore produces better answers for users
Pick whichever configuration was evaluated first because earlier runs are less likely to have been tuned
Average the two configurations' scores together so a joint value represents both memories

stem: Version v1 and version v2 of a memory-enabled agent were run through `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` on the same dataset. A reviewer wants to see exactly how the memory change altered the answer to one request. Which TWO steps in the MLflow UI do that? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Delete the v1 run so that the UI shows only the v2 traces as the baseline that is left for the dataset
Open only the v2 run's trace list and rely on the reviewer's recollection of what the v1 answer looked like
Click the request identifier in the comparison to open the full trace of that request from each selected run
Compare the two runs' experiment-level average scores and treat any gap as the explanation for that request
Check the boxes for both runs in Evaluation runs and choose Compare from the Actions drop-down menu

stem: Across repeated MLflow evaluation runs, config P injects ten memory items per request and config Q injects three. Both reach about the same correctness and groundedness, but P's traces show far larger inputs and slower responses. Which configuration is the better context choice?

choices.text: Config P, because response time is not a property of the context configuration
Config P, because injecting more items is safer even if correctness does not improve
Neither, because equal scores mean that the memory injection has no effect on quality and should be removed entirely
Config Q, because it reaches the same quality with a leaner context and less attention budget

stem: A concierge agent always needs the traveler's name, home airport, language and loyalty tier for every request, and these fields are stable columns on one Lakebase row. Which retrieval approach to this memory is best?

choices.text: Retrieve the profile only after the model replies, then append it to the answer text
Static retrieval: query the profile row before the model call and place the small fixed block in the prompt every time
Dynamic retrieval only: give the model a tool and let it decide whether to look up the profile on each request
Run a semantic search over the whole memory store on each request and take whatever ranks highest

stem: A voice assistant has a strict latency budget. Traces show that on nearly every call the agent first calls a memory lookup tool that runs the same query for the caller's next appointment (one small Lakebase row) and only then answers. The tool round trip is the slowest step. What is the best change?

choices.text: Run that fixed appointment query before the model call and place the row in the prompt; keep the tool for rare memories
Make the tool return every stored memory for the caller so that a second lookup is never needed later
Cache the model's final answers per caller for a day so that repeated calls skip memory and retrieval
Keep the lookup tool as it is and lengthen its description so that the model calls it with less hesitation

stem: A team moves an agent from static memory injection to a dynamic memory lookup tool on Lakebase. Which TWO trade-offs should they expect? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Tool descriptions can stay vague, because the model reads the memory store's contents on its own
Each lookup adds a tool-call round trip, so requests that use memory take longer than a preloaded block
Recall improves over static injection, because the model calls the tool whenever memory could help
Context size stays fixed, because the tool returns the same number of tokens for each question asked
The agent may skip the lookup or phrase a poor query, which can leave relevant memories out of the context

stem: A banking assistant has a small set of facts it needs on every turn (customer segment, preferred channel) and a large history of past service notes that matter only occasionally. Which retrieval design best balances predictability and token cost?

choices.text: Retrieve both sets statically before every model call so that nothing depends on the model's decisions
Retrieve both sets dynamically so that the model decides about the segment and channel as well
Skip retrieval for the small facts and rely on the model to infer them from the wording of the question
Use static retrieval for the small always-needed facts and dynamic retrieval for the large occasional history

stem: An assistant retrieves user memories dynamically through a lookup tool on Lakebase. Traces show that on questions about the user's earlier decisions, the agent answers directly without calling the tool, so personalization is missing. Which change addresses this with the least extra context?

choices.text: Replace the tool with a larger system prompt that repeats each memory category in full on each turn
State in the tool description what it returns and when to call it, or preload the few always-needed fields
Remove the lookup tool and ask the model to recall earlier decisions from its general training knowledge
Preload all stored memories for the user into every prompt so that the tool call is no longer needed

stem: A travel agent injects the 25 closest memories from its Lakebase-backed memory store into every request. As the store grew, answers got worse: asked to rebook a flight, the agent quoted a seat preference from a hotel stay two years ago and ignored the new date. The trace shows only 3 of the 25 injected memories relate to flights. Which diagnosis and fix fit best?

choices.text: Under-retrieval, because the agent ignored the new date, so raise the number of injected memories until the date appears again
A weak embedding model, so re-embed the whole memory store with a larger model and keep injecting all 25 closest memories
Over-retrieval that pollutes the window, so cap the injected memories and require a relevance score before a memory enters the prompt
Context clash, because the memories contradict each other, so delete the older memories and keep only the newest 25 entries

stem: A meal-planning agent recalls memories through a lookup that returns only items whose similarity score passes a very strict threshold. A user said in an earlier conversation, "I'm vegetarian," and the fact is in the memory store. In a new conversation the agent proposes a steak dinner. The trace shows the memory search span returned zero results for "what should I cook tonight". What is the failure and the best change?

choices.text: A pipeline delay, so schedule the memory pipeline to run more often and then re-run the same strict retrieval afterwards
Under-retrieval, so relax the threshold or query with the user's constraints, then confirm the memory returns
Memory poisoning, so rewrite the stored fact as an instruction in the system prompt and delete the entry from the memory store for good
Over-retrieval, so lower the number of results returned and keep the strict threshold so fewer memories are used

stem: An engineer compares two agent traces to tell over-retrieval from under-retrieval in a memory system. Which TWO observations point to over-retrieval? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The memory search returns one item, and the answer uses it correctly and cites the stored detail
Input tokens per model call keep rising as the store grows, although the kind of questions has not changed
The memory search returns no items, and the agent asks the user for a preference already in the store
The answer lacks a fact that exists in the store but was missing from the list the memory search returned
The search returns twenty items, the answer uses two, and an unrelated item's detail shows up in it

stem: To stop context pollution, a team cuts memory retrieval from 10 results to 2. The evaluation dataset now shows fewer unrelated details in answers, but questions that need three separate stored facts (diet, budget, dates) lose accuracy. Which next step best balances both failures?

choices.text: Return to 10 results and accept the pollution, since recall failures cost more than extra tokens in most tasks
Set a relevance score gate with a moderate cap, then re-run the evaluation for unrelated details and missing facts
Keep 2 results and ask users to repeat the missing facts, since the store is not designed for multi-fact questions
Run the memory search a second time per question and inject both result sets, doubling the retrieved text per turn

stem: A wellness agent stores each past conversation transcript as one memory entry. For a question about the user's sleep goal, retrieval returns three entries that are about two thousand tokens each; the goal is a single sentence inside one of them. Most of the returned text is unrelated chat. Which change reduces over-retrieval without losing the goal?

choices.text: Distill conversations into short durable facts, one entry per goal, and retrieve those instead of whole transcripts
Make each stored entry larger so the goal and its surrounding conversation are always retrieved together as one block
Return a single transcript entry per question and hope the closest one contains the goal sentence
Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore unrelated chat inside each retrieved memory entry

stem: A shopping agent's memory pipeline runs nightly. After months of use, one customer's memory store holds about forty near-identical entries such as "prefers aisle seats" and "likes aisle seat", and retrieval of the top five fills with these copies while the customer's allergy note ranks sixth and never reaches the prompt. Which change fits best?

choices.text: Have the memory pipeline consolidate duplicate facts into one durable entry each when it distills the sessions
Raise the retrieval count to fifty, so that the allergy note is always among the injected memories
Add a system prompt line telling the model that repeated preferences are not important to the customer
Delete the whole memory store each week and let the agent rebuild its preferences from new chats

stem: An engineer deletes an entire session store that belonged to a retired version of a support agent, to clean up. A product owner worries that every user's saved preferences will disappear and that the agent will start over with each person. What actually happens?

choices.text: Preferences stay but become read-only until a new session store with the same name is created
Preferences are lost, because memory is stored as a child object of the session store and is removed with it
Preferences stay, because deleting a session or a session store does not delete memory kept in a memory store
Preferences are lost, because the memory pipeline automatically rebuilds the memory store from sessions that no longer exist

stem: A shopping agent writes memories keyed by the current chat ID. A customer who set a size preference on Monday opens a new chat on Wednesday, and the agent shows no knowledge of it, although the memory entry exists. What configuration change fixes the recall?

choices.text: Make the embeddings more precise so Monday's chat ID is matched against Wednesday's chat ID
Retain each chat longer, so Wednesday's chat can load Monday's chat in full as its session state
Write the preference again at the start of each chat with a tool call, so every chat holds its own copy
Scope memories to the customer as the subject rather than to a chat, so any later conversation can recall them

stem: A team is starting a new agent that needs sessions and long-term memory on Databricks. Their wiki recommends the earlier managed agent memory store governed by Unity Catalog. Which choice matches current Databricks guidance for a new agent?

choices.text: Use the earlier managed memory store, because Unity Catalog governance makes it the recommended memory approach
Use Lakebase-backed agent sessions and agent memory, with a memory pipeline to distill sessions into memories
Build both on Delta files only, because Lakebase-backed stores cannot be used with other frameworks
Store memories as rows in the agent's own prompt template so that no store needs configuring

stem: A multi-tenant support agent keeps durable memories for thousands of customers in Databricks agent memory. Security requires that a customer's memories are only ever recalled for that customer and that only the right identities can touch the stores. Which TWO configuration practices satisfy this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Give all agents read access to every store so that a future agent can reuse any memory without a new grant
Merge the session store and the memory store into one store so that a single permission covers both
Put every customer's memories in one shared space and instruct the model in the prompt never to mention other customers
Grant access to the session and memory stores only to the identities that need them, using the store permission controls
Scope each memory to the customer as its subject and recall only that subject's memories when a request arrives

stem: In a support agent, a user writes "What did they decide about it?" after discussing a vendor contract earlier in the same conversation. The agent embeds the raw message, searches memory and receives unrelated items about other vendors. Where in the pipeline should the fix be applied?

choices.text: Resolve the intent first by using the session to turn "they" and "it" into a standalone query, then retrieve
Let the model read all returned items first and silently pick the right vendor from them
Increase the number of memories retrieved so that the right vendor decision is more likely to be among them
Fine-tune the embedding model on short messages that contain pronouns, such as "they" and "it"

stem: An engineer sketches four stages for an agent that answers from memory and tables. Which order puts intent resolution where the exam expects it?

choices.text: Receive message, retrieve with the raw text, inject the results, resolve intent from what was retrieved
Resolve intent from the retrieved items, receive the message, inject the results, retrieve with the raw text
Receive message with session state, resolve intent, retrieve with the resolved query, inject the results
Receive message, inject the entire memory store, retrieve what remains useful, resolve intent last

stem: An assistant is asked, "Show me the numbers for Apollo." The company has both a project and a customer called Apollo. Retrieval returns budget memos for the project and billing notes for the customer, and the answer blends them. The conversation gives no hint which is meant. What is the best fix in the pipeline?

choices.text: Add a metadata column labelled "apollo" to every document so that retrieval can match both meanings more exactly
Detect the ambiguity at the intent stage and ask a clarifying question or use session context before retrieving
Retrieve both sets, then add a system prompt line that tells the model to pick whichever Apollo seems more likely, and answer
Increase the result count so the answer can quote both Apollos and let the user sort out the mix

stem: A team adds an intent-resolution step to their memory agent. Which TWO benefits can they expect from resolving intent before retrieval? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The memory pipeline can store raw transcripts, since intent resolution cleans them at write time
Retrieval no longer needs evaluating, because a resolved query always returns exactly the right memories
The agent can route a request to the right source, such as a structured query for a stored field or semantic search for a vague recollection
The agent can answer without retrieving at all, because every question is understood well enough to guess
The retrieval query matches what the user means, so fewer irrelevant memories are pulled into the window

stem: A team adds a model call that rewrites every user message into a standalone query before memory retrieval. Latency rose noticeably. Their logs show that most messages are already self-contained, such as "What is my current plan tier?", while a minority use pronouns or name clashes. What is the best adjustment?

choices.text: Keep the model call but cache each rewrite for a year, so repeated messages never trigger a new call
Move the rewrite after retrieval so it can use the returned memories to decide what the user meant
Remove the resolution step entirely, since most messages do not need it and the few that do are acceptable losses
Run resolution only for ambiguous messages, such as unresolved references or several matches, and retrieve directly otherwise

stem: An agent connects to three MCP servers: a GitHub server, a Slack server and a custom server on Databricks Apps. Together they expose dozens of tools, and the trace shows every model call starting with all tool names, descriptions and parameter schemas, most of which are never used in a request. Which change applies progressive disclosure best?

choices.text: Remove two of the three servers from the agent for good and keep the one used most often
Show a short server catalog with each one's purpose, then load a server's tool schemas only when the agent picks it
Cut every tool description to one word so the same full list costs fewer tokens in each call
Move the full tool list into the system prompt so that the model provider can cache it across calls, keeping every tool

stem: A finance agent calls a generic SQL tool on a custom MCP server for "Which three regions had the highest gross margin last quarter?". stem: A research agent is close to its context limit. The history holds a 30,000-character JSON result from `get_orders`, returned 25 turns ago. Pleasantries and acknowledgments, which carry no information and should be restored so that the agent keeps a natural and friendly tone with users
Duplicate tool results, whose first copy should have been removed instead of the last copy that the agent needed

stem: An agent's wrapper appends a debug line to every tool result, such as `latency_ms=412 tokens=1860 request_id=7f3a`. Those lines make up a sizeable share of the history, and no later step ever reads them. The same information is also recorded by MLflow Tracing. Can they be removed during compaction?

choices.text: Yes, but only after the agent has repeated each figure in its own words so that a copy of each remains
No, because latency and token figures can change the agent's choice of tool, so they must remain in the history
No, because request ids must stay in the history to let the agent resend a request when a call fails
Yes, because the agent never uses them, and MLflow Tracing already records latency, token usage and cost for each step

stem: A team plans to remove a new category of content, retrieved reference passages that the agent quotes in earlier answers, from compacted histories. It wants evidence that this is safe before it goes into production. Which check gives the strongest evidence?

choices.text: Count how many tokens the passages use, since a category that uses the most tokens is the most likely to be safe to remove
Remove the category only from the oldest turns of each trace, because the oldest content is the least likely to matter in later steps
Replay saved traces with the category removed and compare the downstream steps and final answers with the originals, looking for changes
Ask the model in the agent whether it believes it needs the passages, and remove them if it says that it does not

stem: A triage agent classifies thousands of low-stakes support tickets per hour. Each ticket needs only the last few messages, a missed detail costs a minor re-ask, and token spend is the main complaint. Which compaction posture fits?

choices.text: Conservative compaction in the first half of each session and no compaction afterward, so that the cost stays predictable for the whole team
Aggressive compaction that compresses hard, because the risk of losing subtle context is cheap and the savings are large at this volume
Conservative compaction that preserves nearly every detail, since fidelity is always more important than token cost
No compaction, with every message kept in the window, so that the agent never loses detail in a high-volume setting

stem: A claims agent reviews insurance cases over many turns. A missed exclusion clause or a qualifier such as "only if filed within the policy year" can lead to a wrong payout. Token cost is moderate and volume is low. Which compaction posture fits best?

choices.text: No summary of any kind and a hard cap on the number of turns, so that the case ends before the context grows
Aggressive compaction with a short summary, because the cost of the agent per case is the main factor in the decision
Aggressive compaction followed by a human review of every summary, since people can add back the details the summarizer lost in the process
Conservative compaction that keeps clauses, qualifiers and exceptions verbatim, accepting a higher token cost for a lower risk of a costly error

stem: A team compares an aggressive compaction prompt with a conservative one for the same agent. Which TWO statements correctly describe the trade-off? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Aggressive compaction lowers the tokens carried on every later call, but it raises the chance of losing a subtle qualifier or exception
Conservative compaction guarantees correct answers, since a summary that keeps more detail can never confuse or distract the agent
Conservative compaction is cheaper per call, since the summary keeps more text that the cache can reuse across long sessions without charge
Aggressive compaction removes the need to evaluate downstream accuracy, because less content in the summary leaves less that can be wrong
Conservative compaction keeps higher fidelity, but the longer summaries cost more tokens on each call and fill the attention budget sooner

stem: A long-running legal-research agent reads dozens of documents. Aggressive compaction made it cheap but it sometimes lost an exception clause. Conservative compaction fixed that but doubled token cost. The team wants most of the savings and keeps the safety. Which design best balances them?

choices.text: Run conservative compaction on every call, and halve the number of documents the agent reads in each session
Compact aggressively, but keep critical categories such as clauses, exceptions and constraints verbatim, and compress routine narrative hard
Switch to aggressive compaction for the first half of each task and conservative in the second half, so that older material is compressed hard
Alternate between the two postures on a timer, aggressive in odd turns and conservative in even turns, to average the cost

stem: A team must decide how aggressive its compaction should be for a new agent. They have 200 saved tasks and can run MLflow 3 evaluation on traces, which record token usage and cost for each step. Which approach gives the best basis for the decision?

choices.text: Pick the setting that gives the shortest summaries, because token usage is the only figure that a trace records for each step of the agent run
Pick the setting that most closely matches that of a similar agent, since compaction posture does not depend on the task
Run the same tasks at several compaction levels, compare task success with token cost, and choose the cheapest level that meets the bar
Ask three reviewers which summaries read best, and choose the level that most of them pick as the best written

stem: A coordinating agent splits a vendor contract review between a pricing sub-agent and a legal sub-agent. The pricing agent recommends accepting a 25 percent discount, while the legal agent, working at the same time, flags that discounts above 15 percent need executive approval and recommends against it. Neither saw the other's work. What is the best diagnosis?

choices.text: The pricing agent ran too early, so the fix is to run all the sub-agents in sequence with a longer waiting time between steps in the plan
The orchestrator's context is too small, so the answer is a longer window for the coordinator to hold both outputs together
The agents work from different assumptions with no shared context, so their decisions conflict and the cap should reach both
The model of the legal agent is too cautious, so it should be replaced by one that gives fewer conflicting recommendations

stem: Three writer sub-agents each draft one section of a quarterly report. The coordinator gets back three sections that look fine alone, but one uses calendar quarters, another fiscal quarters, and the third uses "revenue" to mean net where the others mean gross. Each sub-agent received only its own section assignment. What is the root cause?

choices.text: The writers' temperature settings were too high, and lowering them would make all three agents choose the same convention
No definitions or conventions were shared with the sub-agents, so each filled the gaps differently and the outputs were inconsistent
The coordinator should have merged the three sections itself into one, since consistent output is only possible with a single writer
The sub-agents' context windows were too small to read their section assignments, so they guessed the missing details

stem: A multi-agent workflow has failures in production. Which TWO observations are symptoms of insufficient shared context between agents? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Two sub-agents reach opposite decisions about the same customer because each assumed a different policy that the other agent never saw
One sub-agent fails with a timeout because the external API it calls is slow, and the other sub-agents finish their work normally
The coordinator's total token cost is high because it makes many calls, although each call uses the data and rules it is meant to use
One sub-agent returns a malformed response because a model call hit a transient service error that is gone on the next retry
Sub-agent outputs use different names for the same entity, so the coordinator has to reconcile them before it can combine the results

stem: In a supplier-onboarding workflow, a verification sub-agent calls an external registry and confirms a supplier's tax id. A compliance sub-agent, dispatched at the same time, makes the same registry call and reports the id as unverified because its call was rate-limited. The final answer is contradictory. What does the failure show about the workflow?

choices.text: The registry limit is the root cause, so raising it would let both sub-agents call it together and remove the contradiction for good
The compliance sub-agent needs a longer window, so that it can hold several retries of the registry call in one conversation
The compliance sub-agent has no real task of its own, because two agents should never work on the same supplier in one workflow
The verification finding was not visible to the compliance sub-agent, so it repeated the work and reached a different result from its own call

stem: A multi-agent trip planner has a flight agent, a hotel agent and an itinerary agent. Occasionally the itinerary agent books a hotel for dates that differ from the flight dates, and reruns of the same request give different results. Traces show that the flight agent decided on the dates in its own context, while the hotel agent inferred dates from the original request. What is the root cause?

choices.text: The hotel agent reads the request carelessly, so a stricter instruction to quote the dates word for word would stop the date mismatch
A decision that other agents depend on stayed in one agent's context, so each of the others inferred it and the inferences varied between runs
The itinerary agent lacks authority to override the other agents, so a vote across the three outputs would settle the dates reliably
The request is too short for any agent to plan from, so the user should be asked for more detail before each run of the workflow

stem: A coordinating agent plans a customer-refund workflow and dispatches a drafting sub-agent with the message "Write the reply for ticket 4411". During planning, the coordinator's trace recorded that the customer is on a legacy contract and that the standard refund policy was ruled out. The drafted reply quotes the standard policy. What is the root cause?

choices.text: The drafting sub-agent's model is too weak to follow a refund policy, so a larger model is needed to read the ticket text and the contract type correctly
The coordinator planned too many steps, so it should merge all sub-agents into one agent that handles every step in sequence
The sub-agent got only an individual task message, not the trace, so earlier decisions were invisible
The task message was too short, so adding a second sentence of instruction would let the sub-agent infer the contract type

stem: A multi-agent Databricks workflow suffers from downstream failures because sub-agents get only task messages. The coordinator's trace is long, and each sub-agent already runs near its attention budget, so the window cannot be made larger. Which dispatch configuration resolves the failure?

choices.text: Switch the sub-agents to a model with a larger context window so that the entire raw coordinator trace can be pasted in front of each task message
Dispatch with the task message plus the last few coordinator messages only, because the most recent messages always hold the key decisions
Keep the task messages and let each sub-agent ask the user a clarifying question whenever a needed decision is missing from its message
Dispatch each sub-agent with a compacted version of the coordinator's trace, keeping decisions, constraints and results, in place of the bare task message

stem: A coordinator dispatches four sub-agents, and a reviewer suspects that the downstream failures come from missing context at dispatch. The team records MLflow traces for the whole workflow. Which check in the traces best confirms that diagnosis?

choices.text: Compare the input recorded on each sub-agent's span with the decisions and results in the coordinator's earlier steps, looking for what never reached the sub-agent
Compare the latency of the sub-agent spans and treat the slowest one as the place where its context was lost during the workflow run
Check that every sub-agent span records the same model name, because a mixed set of models is the usual cause of inconsistent downstream results
Count the tokens in each sub-agent's output and flag the sub-agents that returned the longest answers as the source of the downstream failures

stem: A coordinator has a trace with many turns of exploration. A sub-agent that writes a SQL query needs only the schema decisions and the agreed business definitions from that trace. The team wants to fix failures caused by task-message-only dispatch without enlarging the sub-agent's window. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Dispatch only the task message, and rely on the sub-agent's tools to rediscover the schema decisions on its own
Dispatch the unfiltered trace, since a sub-agent that sees everything can decide for itself which parts apply to its task
Dispatch the part of the trace that carries the schema decisions and definitions, in condensed form, with the task message on top
Dispatch a fixed number of the oldest trace messages, since early messages contain the original instructions and definitions

stem: A coordinator dispatches sub-agents with individual task messages, and downstream failures follow. The team has decided that sub-agent context windows must stay the same size. Which TWO changes address the failure within that limit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Include a compacted summary of the coordinator's decisions and results in what each sub-agent receives at dispatch
Remove all earlier tool results from the coordinator so that its trace is empty when the sub-agents are started
Move every sub-agent to a model that has a larger context window so the full trace can be added to their input
Write a longer task message for each sub-agent that repeats the complete original user request and nothing else
Pass each sub-agent only the portion of the trace that is relevant to its own sub-task, not the whole trace

stem: A coordinator dispatches a forecasting sub-agent and a staffing sub-agent in parallel. The forecasting agent assumes 12 percent demand growth, while the staffing agent works from flat demand, so the plan contradicts itself. Which context propagation change would most likely prevent this?

choices.text: Give each sub-agent a longer list of tools so that it can search for the demand assumption on its own
Have the forecasting agent finish first and pass its assumptions to the staffing agent at dispatch
Ask the staffing agent to review the forecasting agent's final report in a later pass, after both agents have finished their own work and returned results
Run both agents with a lower sampling temperature so that their assumptions become more similar between runs

stem: A report coordinator dispatches an analysis agent and later a summary agent. The summary agent receives the analysis agent's conclusion ("margin is acceptable") but not the assumption behind it (excludes returns). Its summary then recommends a discount that the full analysis rules out. Which propagation change most reduces this conflict?

choices.text: Pass only one-word conclusions between agents to avoid any clutter in the receiving agent's context
Have the summary agent re-run the analysis agent's query to infer for itself which assumptions were used
Increase the summary agent's temperature so that it explores more alternatives before settling on a recommendation
Pass each sub-agent's conclusion together with the assumptions and constraints it relied on to the agents that build on it

stem: A user tells a coordinator at the start: "Exclude customers in the EU from every figure." The coordinator paraphrases the request separately for three analysis sub-agents. One paraphrase leaves out the exclusion, and the combined totals clash. Which propagation change most likely prevents the conflict in later runs?

choices.text: Rerun the analysis sub-agent that ignored the exclusion until its total happens to come close to the totals of the other two sub-agents
Pass the user's constraint verbatim, as one shared block, to every sub-agent whose output feeds the combined totals
Have the coordinator merge the three outputs and subtract the EU amounts that it estimates from the result of the agent that ignored the exclusion
Tell every analysis sub-agent to search the stored chat history by itself for any user constraint before it begins its own analysis

stem: Two sub-agents handle different parts of a customer case and both write recommendations to the coordinator. After the first agent's recommendation, the customer's plan was changed, and the second agent still used the old plan in its work. What propagation change would most likely prevent this conflict?

choices.text: Send the coordinator's full history of all events to every agent, whether current or outdated, without marking which entries are still valid and which are replaced
Let the second agent keep the older plan, since each agent should stay with the information it received first
Tell every agent to ignore any information that was changed after the task started, to keep the outputs stable
Keep a shared decision record where a newer entry supersedes the older, and give agents the current record

stem: A planner agent assigns a build task to a coding sub-agent and a test task to a testing sub-agent at the same time. The testing agent writes tests for function names that the coding agent renamed, and the results contradict. Which context propagation change is best?

choices.text: Ask the testing agent to write tests more generally, so that function names do not matter for the tests
Give both agents the same long description of the entire project, so that both can guess the new names the same way
Share the interface decisions (names and signatures) from the coding agent with the testing agent before it writes tests
Let the testing agent search the repository once the work is done and fix any test that fails because of the names

stem: In a Databricks workflow, an orchestrating agent calls five research sub-agents. Each returns its full raw tool output and reasoning, and the orchestrator's context saturates before it can synthesize. Which sub-agent output design most reduces the orchestrator's load without losing task coherence?

choices.text: Return a structured summary with the findings, key values and open issues, and keep the full output outside the orchestrator's context
Return everything unchanged but ask the orchestrator to compress it later, after the synthesis step is already complete
Return the raw output in several smaller messages so that the orchestrator reads each message separately and forgets earlier ones
Return only a yes or no verdict from each sub-agent, because the orchestrator can ask follow-up questions if it needs more

stem: A document-analysis orchestrator is saturated after receiving long narrative answers from its sub-agents. After a team switched to one-word verdicts, the context load dropped but the final report lost its supporting figures and contradictions between documents went unnoticed. Which redesign balances load and coherence?

choices.text: Require a fixed output schema with the verdict, supporting figures, document references and conflicts found, and nothing else
Let each sub-agent choose its own output format, since the agents know best which details deserve to be passed on
Keep the one-word verdicts and have the orchestrator re-read each source document when it needs the figures
Return to the long narrative answers but increase the number of sub-agents so that each one writes a shorter narrative

stem: A coordinating agent receives research from sub-agents whose full findings run to many pages. The coordinator needs to cite sources and can rarely use the complete text. Which design change lowers its context load while keeping the evidence reachable?

choices.text: Have each sub-agent return only the summary and delete the full findings afterwards, which keeps the storage small and the design simple for the team
Have the coordinator ask every sub-agent for the same findings again whenever a citation is requested by the user
Have each sub-agent include the full findings as well as the summary, so the coordinator can pick whichever it prefers
Have each sub-agent store the full findings as an artifact and return a short summary plus a reference to it

stem: An orchestrator coordinates several sub-agents and runs out of context. The team wants sub-agent output designs that reduce the orchestrator's load without compromising coherence. Which TWO designs should it adopt? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Return output in whichever format each sub-agent prefers, because that avoids rework in the sub-agents themselves
Return the complete intermediate reasoning of each sub-agent so that the orchestrator can verify every step by itself
Return the full result to external storage and give the orchestrator a summary with a pointer to the stored data
Return only a status code, because the orchestrator can reconstruct the conclusions from the status of each sub-agent
Return a result in an agreed structure, with conclusions, key values and unresolved questions, and exclude the process narrative

stem: An orchestrator receives results from parallel sub-agents. Even though each result is a short paragraph, the orchestrator still saturates when many sub-agents run, and the paragraphs repeat the original task description at length. Which output design change would reduce the load most while keeping coherence?

choices.text: Ask sub-agents to return their results in whichever language uses the fewest tokens for the model, so that every result takes less space in the window
Drop restated task text and return only new information in a consistent structure
Add more detail to each paragraph so that the orchestrator never has to ask the sub-agent anything else
Merge all sub-agents into one so that their results no longer need to be returned to a separate orchestrator

stem: A multi-agent design uses one agent to write a SQL transformation and another to validate it. Traces show that every handoff needs a very long summary of the writer's reasoning, and the validator still asks the writer for clarification. Which boundary placement failure is occurring?

choices.text: The validator's context window is too large, so it reads unrelated material that the writer's summary happened to include
The agents have been placed too far apart in the workflow, so the number of other agents between them causes the overhead
The writer and validator should have been given more tools, because handoff overhead only occurs when an agent has too few tools
The boundary cuts through a tightly coupled task, so handoffs need large summaries and still lose detail the validator needs

stem: A single "operations" agent handles data research, report writing, compliance checking and customer replies. Its trace shows that the context grows with every request, older tool results from unrelated tasks stay in the window, and answers get less accurate over time. Which boundary placement failure and fix apply?

choices.text: The agent has too few instructions; adding a long prompt covering all the responsibilities would restore accuracy
One agent's boundary covers several independent responsibilities; separate sub-agents with own contexts limit growth
Handoffs are too expensive; merging the agent with the compliance checker would remove the overhead
The model's context window is too small, and replacing it with a larger one is the only possible remedy for the unmanageable growth seen in the trace

stem: A team designed eight narrow agents, one for each tiny step of an invoice workflow (read, parse, validate date, validate amount, post). The trace shows most tokens go into summaries passed between agents, and the posting agent lacks details the parser knew. Which diagnosis and redesign fit?

choices.text: Context windows are too small; each agent needs a larger window to hold the entire invoice and all previous steps
Too few agents exist; splitting each step into even smaller agents would lower the cost of every handoff
Boundaries are too fine-grained, so handoff overhead dominates; combine the steps that depend on each other into fewer agents
The summaries are too short; asking each agent for longer handoffs would prevent the posting agent from missing details

stem: A team reviews a multi-agent architecture for boundary problems. Which TWO observations indicate that a boundary was drawn through tightly coupled work, producing handoff compression overhead? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Handoff summaries are very large because the two agents need most of the same reasoning to do their work
The orchestrator's token cost is high because it handles many independent requests from different users
A sub-agent takes a long time because the external API it calls responds slowly during peak hours
A sub-agent's answers are accurate, and its context contains only material about its own responsibility
The receiving agent repeatedly asks the sending agent for details that did not survive the handoff summary

stem: A research workflow has one agent that reads thirty independent regulatory documents in sequence. By the end its window is full of earlier documents, and it confuses details across them. Another team member suggests a boundary change. Which diagnosis and change are right?

choices.text: Window growth comes from independent documents; give each document or group to a sub-agent and return findings
The summaries are too detailed, so ask the agent to forget each document as soon as it has read it completely
The model does not support reading long documents, so a different retrieval method should replace the documents entirely and permanently in the workflow
Handoff overhead is too high, so merge the document-reading agent with the writer that formats the final report

stem: A long-running Databricks agent must analyze twelve independent data sources and compile findings. It uses one agent that compacts its history as it goes, and quality falls as each source's details crowd out the others. Which replacement strategy fits the task's dependency structure, and why?

choices.text: A larger window with no compaction, because the sources are independent and the agent should keep all their details visible at once
More frequent compaction, because the cause of the failure is the infrequency of summaries between sources
Structured notes written after each source, because notes are the only way to preserve findings in any long task
Sub-agents that each handle one source in an isolated context and return a condensed finding, because the sources do not depend on each other

stem: An agent migrates sixty tables over many hours using compaction. After each compaction it sometimes repeats a finished table or skips one, because the summary states "most tables are done". Each table is a clear milestone, and the exact set of completed tables matters. Which strategy replaces compaction, and why?

choices.text: Trimming the oldest messages, because old completed tables are no longer relevant to the task
Sub-agents per table in parallel, because migrations should always be split by table whatever their dependencies
Structured notes with a persisted progress record, because the exact state of discrete milestones must survive resets
A larger context window, because a bigger window removes the need to track which tables are finished

stem: A team split a debugging task across a hypothesis agent, a test agent and a fix agent, each handing over a summary. Performance fails: every agent restarts reasoning because the key reasoning chain is lost in handoffs. The work is one continuous investigation where each step builds on the last. Which replacement is best?

choices.text: More sub-agents with smaller tasks, because shorter tasks need shorter reasoning chains between handoffs
One agent that keeps the whole investigation and compacts older history as it goes, because each step depends on the previous reasoning
Structured notes only, because notes alone can fully replace the live reasoning of an investigation in progress
Independent sub-agents running in parallel on the same problem, because several separate attempts will each lose less of the reasoning than one chain does

stem: A long-horizon agent writes a large report made of modules. A team used sub-agents for each module, but the modules share a running set of design decisions that each depends on, and results contradict. Which TWO task characteristics make sub-agents with isolated contexts insufficient here? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Later modules build on earlier modules' reasoning, which handoff summaries do not carry fully
The report will be reviewed by a person at the end, so the review should replace any coordination between modules
The modules are long, so each module needs more tokens than the orchestrator can ever receive in one message
The work has no deadline, so the agent can afford any strategy and none of them will matter for quality
Each module depends on decisions made while writing the others, so independent contexts cannot stay consistent

stem: An insurance claims agent on Databricks holds sessions of about 120 turns. After turn 90, requests fail because the input exceeds the model's 128,000-token window. The MLflow trace shows that 70 percent of the input is raw output from policy-lookup tool calls in earlier turns, which the agent has already acted on. Governance allows only the current model, and the 8-second latency budget leaves no room for an extra model call on every turn. Which technique fixes the failure with the LEAST added latency?

choices.text: Move the agent to a model with a one-million-token window, so that the full history of every session fits without changing how tool output is handled
Summarize the whole conversation with a separate model call before every turn, so that the history sent to the agent stays far below the window size
Clear the raw output of tool calls older than the last few turns, leaving a stub that names the tool and its arguments for a repeat call
Shorten the system prompt and its list of rules to free space for history, since instructions are sent again with every request in the session

stem: A finance team is designing a reconciliation agent before its first release. Forty Unity Catalog functions exist in the team schema, but the reconciliation job uses six of them, and two of those six return entire ledgers of up to 50,000 rows. The per-request token budget is 20,000 tokens, and the team wants to prevent context pressure from the start instead of reacting to failures in production. Which TWO design choices are proactive strategies for this agent? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Load both full ledgers into the system prompt at session start, so that the agent never needs a tool call and avoids repeated round trips
Plan to turn on compaction once production traces show the window filling, because summarizing history later costs less than redesigning tools
Give the agent all forty functions and add a system prompt rule telling the model to ignore the functions that do not concern reconciliation
Give the agent only the six functions the reconciliation job needs instead of all forty in the schema, keeping tool definitions small
Change the two ledger functions to return the matched totals and the unmatched rows, with a row limit, instead of the entire ledgers

stem: An inventory agent's MLflow trace for one request shows: step 4, `get_stock('SKU-77')` returns 120 units; step 9, a reservation tool confirms an order of 40 units; step 11, `get_stock('SKU-77')` returns 80 units. The final answer says 120 units are available, and the reasoning at step 12 notes "two different stock figures, using the first". Every tool returned correct data at the time of its call. Which diagnosis and fix fit the evidence while adding the fewest tokens?

choices.text: Context clash: an outdated tool result sits next to its newer replacement, so clear or mark superseded results when a call returns fresh data
Context confusion: too many tools led the agent to call the wrong one, so remove the reservation tool and keep only the stock lookup tool
Context distraction: the long history crowds out what the model knows, so compact the whole history into a summary each time it passes ten steps
Context poisoning: a hallucinated stock figure entered the context and was reused, so add a judge that checks every answer against the stock table

stem: A retail team must compare two versions of its shopping agent on 300 questions taken from last month's production traffic before releasing version 2. Security requires that the evaluation evidence be governed with schema- and table-level access control and be queryable in SQL by auditors. Both versions must be scored with the same criteria so that the results are comparable. Which part of the Databricks stack should carry this work?

choices.text: A custom MCP server that exposes both agent versions as tools, so that a third agent calls each version and reports which answer it prefers
MLflow 3, evaluating both versions with the same scorers on a dataset built from production traces, with traces stored in Unity Catalog tables
Lakebase, writing each version's answers into Postgres tables and letting auditors compare the two answer sets with SQL joins on question text
Unity Catalog volumes, saving each version's answers as JSON files and granting auditors READ VOLUME so that they can open and compare the files

stem: A product-support agent's system prompt is 11,500 tokens: 2,000 tokens of rules and a 9,500-token product catalog appended "for reference". Traces show that the catalog is needed in about 3 percent of requests, and that in other requests the agent drifts into recommending catalog products nobody asked about. The 3 percent of requests that need the catalog require exact SKU and price values. Which change best improves focus without losing those answers?

choices.text: Replace the catalog with a 2,000-token summary of product families, which keeps the general picture in the prompt at a fifth of the size
Keep the catalog in the prompt and add a rule telling the agent to mention products only when the user asks for a recommendation by name
Move the catalog behind a lookup tool that returns entries for the products named in a request, and keep only the rules in the prompt
Move the catalog to the end of the system prompt, so that the rules come first and receive more of the model's attention on every request

stem: A voice assistant for a utility company must start speaking within 2 seconds on routine turns. About 90 percent of turns are simple lookups such as balance or outage status; 10 percent are multi-step billing disputes, where standard mode gives wrong answers and callers are told to hold while the agent works. A rules engine already labels every request with an intent, and the model accepts a per-request reasoning effort setting. Which configuration best balances accuracy, latency and token cost?

choices.text: Send lookup intents with the lowest reasoning effort and billing disputes with a high effort, using the label the rules engine sets
Send every request with a high reasoning effort, since disputes need it and a single setting is simpler to operate than per-intent settings
Send every request with the lowest reasoning effort and add billing examples to the prompt, so disputes improve without extra reasoning tokens
Send every request with a medium reasoning effort as a compromise, accepting slower lookups and only partly improved answers on disputes

stem: An HR assistant keeps the full conversation in context. An MLflow evaluation of long sessions shows that adherence to a rule the user set in turn 2 ("only show figures for my department") drops sharply once the history passes about 60,000 tokens, although the window holds 200,000. Compliance requires the full transcript to be kept for audit. Which intervention restores adherence while meeting the audit requirement?

choices.text: Drop every message older than the last 20 turns from both the model input and the session store, so the history stays below 60,000 tokens
Append the complete conversation so far to the end of each new user message, so that earlier rules appear near the end of the input again
Keep sending the full transcript because the audit rule requires the model to see every message, and move to a model with twice the window
Keep the full transcript in the session store for audit, and send the model a compacted history restating the user's constraints verbatim

stem: A sales Genie Agent already has 92 example SQL queries, 6 SQL functions and one general instructions block, against a limit of 100 instructions per agent. Users want 15 new question patterns answered, each a variation of "sales for <region> in <quarter>", and every answer to them must be shown as a verified answer. Which change meets both the limit and the verification requirement?

choices.text: Define the regional sales logic as SQL expressions in the knowledge store, since snippets count toward a separate limit of 200 per agent
Create a second Genie Agent for the new patterns and tell users which of the two agents to open for regional questions from now on
Describe the fifteen new patterns in the general instructions block, since that whole block counts as one instruction however long it grows
Add one parameterized example SQL query that takes region and quarter as parameters, so all fifteen patterns reuse one verified query

stem: An extraction agent's prompt holds seven few-shot examples of about 300 tokens each. Five exist only to show the exact JSON layout; two show how to handle invoices with credit notes, which the agent used to get wrong. The team must cut the prompt by at least 1,200 tokens without losing accuracy on credit notes, and the serving endpoint supports structured outputs. Which change fits every constraint?

choices.text: Remove the five layout examples and pass the JSON schema through `response_format`, keeping the two credit-note examples in the prompt
Keep all seven examples but cut each to about 120 tokens by removing the invoice text and leaving only the expected JSON output

stem: A retailer's 3,000-token system prompt is used by agents in four regions, and legal must review every changed line. Traces show one failure pattern: the rule "Escalate refunds over $500 to a human" is also applied to store-credit requests, which agents may grant without escalation up to $2,000. Which revision fixes the failure at the LEAST token and maintenance cost?

choices.text: Add six few-shot examples that show store-credit requests being granted without escalation, placed after the rules in the prompt
Rewrite the whole system prompt into region-specific versions, so that each region phrases its refund and credit rules in its own way
Edit that rule to read "Escalate cash refunds over $500 to a human; store credit up to $2,000 needs no escalation"

stem: An MLflow 3 evaluation on 400 questions compares a 900-token system prompt (v1) with a 2,400-token version (v2) that adds a warranty section. Overall Correctness rises from 0.81 to 0.84. Keep v1 for all requests and add the 1,500-token warranty section only to warranty-labeled requests, about 180 extra tokens on average
Adopt v2 but have a model compress its warranty section to 400 tokens, and roll it out without measuring the warranty slice again

stem: A finance Genie Agent fails 14 of 60 benchmark questions. Nine failures mix up `net_rev` and `gross_rev`, which have no Unity Catalog column comments; three use calendar instead of fiscal years; two pick a wrong join path. The team can make one fix this sprint, and it must also help a separate agent that calls a SQL function on the same table. Which fix has the highest impact?

Add Unity Catalog column comments that define `net_rev` and `gross_rev`, stating what each amount includes and excludes
Add a text instruction to the Genie Agent that explains net versus gross revenue in the wording the finance team uses day to day
Add a SQL expression for the fiscal year to the Genie Agent's knowledge store, which every fiscal question in this agent will reuse

stem: A curator is building a churn Genie Agent for customer-success managers. Candidates are 14 tables across bronze, silver and gold; a gold metric view that defines churn rate and net retention by segment; and a Unity Catalog SQL function that computes cohort retention with multi-step logic that no single query captures. Databricks guidance favors a small, focused set of objects. Which TWO objects should the curator add first? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The SQL function for cohort retention, so this multi-step logic runs as a trusted asset whose answers are marked verified
The bronze event tables, so that Genie can compute churn from the raw events when the gold objects do not cover a question
The silver tables behind the metric view, so that Genie can join them back to the metric view whenever it needs more detail
All 14 candidate tables, since the 50-object limit allows them and more data lets Genie answer a wider range of questions
