stem: A support agent queries a Direct Vector Access index of 40 million chunks whose vectors were computed with an older embedding model; that model's serving endpoint is still running. After a code release, the agent embeds its queries with a newer model, and retrieval spans show low-similarity, off-topic chunks for every question. Re-embedding the corpus will take three weeks. Which remediation restores retrieval quality now?

choices.text: Raise `num_results` from 5 to 50, so that the relevant chunks, which now score lower than before, still appear among the results
Switch the index query type to hybrid, so that keyword matching makes up for the different models used to embed queries and chunks
Embed queries with the same model that produced the stored chunk vectors until the corpus has been re-embedded with the newer model
Add the AI Search reranker to every query, so that the reranker model reorders the off-topic results into a useful order for the agent

stem: A pipeline parses policy PDFs from a Unity Catalog volume, chunks them and upserts the chunks into a Direct Vector Access index through the SDK. When a policy is withdrawn, its file is deleted from the volume, yet the agent keeps citing it weeks later. The team wants removals to reach the index automatically, without nightly index rebuilds, and wants the chunk data to stay queryable in SQL. Which design change fixes this?

choices.text: Add an instruction to the agent's system prompt telling it to ignore chunks from policies that the policy team has withdrawn
Keep the Direct Vector Access index and rebuild it from scratch every night from the files that still exist in the volume at that time
Keep the Direct Vector Access index and add a filter on a `withdrawn` flag that the agent's tool code includes in every query it sends
Write chunks to a Delta table with change data feed, delete a withdrawn file's rows there, and serve them through a Delta Sync index

stem: A sales-enablement agent answers questions from 4,000 slide decks exported to a Unity Catalog volume, about 30 slides per deck and 60 to 120 tokens per slide, each slide with its own title. The pipeline joins each deck's text and cuts fixed 1,000-token chunks embedded with `databricks-gte-large-en`. Questions target one fact on one slide, such as "which discount tier applies to three-year renewals". Retrieval spans show the right chunk at rank nine or lower, holding ten slides on unrelated topics. Which chunking change best fits the documents and the questions?

choices.text: Keep the 1,000-token chunks and add 30 percent overlap between neighbors, so that facts near chunk edges appear in two chunks
Chunk one slide at a time, prefixing each chunk with its deck title and slide title, so that each vector stands for one topic
Raise the chunk size to 4,000 tokens, which the 8,192-token embedding window allows, so that fewer chunks compete in the ranking
Switch to `databricks-bge-large-en` and cut fixed 512-token chunks, so that each chunk covers about half as many slides as now

stem: A data-engineering agent receives the task "Backfill `sales.orders` for last week" and must run a backfill job. Unity Catalog grants block writes to any other table, and the context budget for task setup is 3,000 tokens. Candidates are the target table with its partition range, a success check (row counts must match the source), the DDL of all 40 tables in the schema (18,000 tokens), 30 days of job logs (25,000 tokens) and the 9,000-token team runbook. Which TWO elements should go into the agent's context? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The target table name with the exact partition range to backfill, which defines the scope of the task the agent must carry out
The last 30 days of job logs, so that the agent can learn from earlier runs which partitions failed before and for which reasons
The DDL of all 40 tables in the schema, so that the agent knows every column it could possibly need while it runs the job
The full team runbook, so that the agent has every procedure the team follows for backfills and for other pipeline jobs as well
The success check that row counts must match the source for every backfilled partition, which defines when the task is done

stem: A code-review agent helps engineers in a monorepo where hundreds of files change every hour. A pre-inference step retrieves chunks from an AI Search index that syncs nightly, and reviews often quote functions that were renamed that morning. Keeping the index in continuous sync would exceed the team's budget, and a single review may take up to a minute. Which retrieval approach should the team choose?

choices.text: Pre-inference retrieval from the same index with more chunks per request, so that renamed functions are more likely to be among the results
Pre-inference retrieval with the index switched to continuous sync, so that every chunk the agent receives reflects changes within minutes
Just-in-time retrieval, giving the agent search and file-read tools over the live repository so it loads the files it needs as it reviews
Load the entire repository into the agent's context at the start of each review, so that it always sees the current version of every file

stem: An MLflow 3 evaluation of a support agent shows high `RetrievalRelevance` but low `RetrievalSufficiency` on questions about the Japan and Korea markets. The retriever queries an index synced from `kb.gold.articles`, the certified table that the steward publishes. Unity Catalog shows that the regional articles live only in `kb.regional.articles`, which is not certified and is excluded from the gold table. Policy allows agents to retrieve only from certified sources. Which action resolves the failure?

choices.text: Raise `num_results` on the existing index, so that the retriever returns enough chunks to cover the regional questions on its own
Grant the agent's service principal read access to the regional schema and let it read the regional articles with a file tool
Point the agent's retriever at a second index synced from `kb.regional.articles`, since the regional teams wrote and approved those articles
Have the steward review the regional articles and publish the approved ones into the certified gold table, so the existing index syncs them

stem: A field-service agent uses a Lakebase-backed session store, and engineers ask it questions such as "What did we decide about the pump at site 14 last quarter?" The team's retention policy clears sessions after 30 days, so answers about older decisions are missing, although the decisions were discussed in those sessions. Security will not approve memory-writing tools inside the agent. Which memory strategy fixes the mismatch?

choices.text: Extend session retention to five years and have the agent replay every earlier session of the user at the start of each new session

Put the last 30 days of session transcripts in the system prompt, so that the agent always has the most recent decisions in context
Run a memory pipeline over the session store that distills durable decisions into a memory store the agent searches semantically

stem: A month-end close agent runs as a Lakeflow job over three days. It posts accrual journal entries, a side effect that must never run twice, and a crash restarts the job from the top. Auditors must be able to see in SQL which steps are complete. Today the agent tracks its progress in a scratchpad inside its context. Which design meets these requirements?

choices.text: Store the scratchpad in the session store, so that the restarted job replays the earlier conversation and infers which steps finished
Save the scratchpad to the memory store, so that the agent recalls completed steps through semantic search when the job starts again
Record each step's status in a Delta table right after the step succeeds, and check that table before any step after a restart
Keep the scratchpad in context and compact it into a summary at the end of every day, so that it survives until the close is finished

stem: A physiotherapy assistant persists memories in Lakebase with `user_id`, `created_at` and free-text `note` columns, and the notes are also indexed in AI Search. A user asks, "What did I tell you about my knee last spring?" The notes use varied wording such as "ACL strain" and "left leg pain". Answers must never include other users' notes, and the context budget for memories is 1,500 tokens. Which retrieval meets the requirements?

choices.text: A SQL query on Lakebase that returns every note of the caller from last spring, placed in context so that the model finds the knee notes
Semantic search over the notes, filtered on the caller's `user_id` and a `created_at` range for last spring, returning top matches

stem: A team compares two memory configurations for an agent. In MLflow 3, config M scored 0.86 Correctness and config N scored 0.79. Opening the runs shows that M was evaluated on dataset version 3 with Correctness and Guidelines judges, while N was evaluated on version 2 with Correctness only; version 3 dropped 40 hard multi-session questions. Each configuration has one run. The team must pick the more reliable configuration. What should it do next?

choices.text: Re-run both configurations on the same dataset version with the same judges, over several runs each, and compare those results
Choose config M, because its Correctness score is seven points higher and it was also checked with an additional Guidelines judge
Raise N's score in proportion to the share of hard questions in version 2, and compare that adjusted score with M's result
Choose config N, because it was evaluated on the older dataset version that still contained the harder multi-session questions

stem: A delivery assistant injects the customer's profile (address, delivery window, language) from a Lakebase row into the prompt once, at session start. Customers sometimes change their address in the mobile app mid-session, and the agent then books deliveries to the old address. The profile read takes about 5 ms, and a trace review showed the model often skips optional lookup tools. Which change fixes the stale-profile failures?

choices.text: Replace the injection with a profile lookup tool that the model may call whenever it thinks the address could have changed meanwhile
Copy the profile into the session store at session start, so that the agent reads it from the conversation state instead of the database
Re-read the profile row by its key before every model call and inject it, keeping the injection static rather than driven by the model
Keep the injection at session start and add a rule telling the agent to ask the customer to confirm the address before every booking

stem: A wellness agent injects the 10 nearest memories from its memory store into every turn, including greetings and small talk. Traces show answers that bring up a user's medical notes in unrelated chats, and the memory block averages 2,800 tokens. Questions that truly need memory use at most three items. Which TWO changes reduce this context pollution without causing under-retrieval? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Retrieve memories only on turns where the request needs personal context, using an intent check before retrieval
Keep ten memories on every turn but move the memory block to the very end of the prompt, right after the latest user message
Store all of the user's memories in the system prompt, so that the agent no longer needs any retrieval step of its own
Cut retrieval to a single memory on every turn, so that at most one unrelated note can ever reach the agent's context
Pass on only memories above a relevance score threshold, and cap the result at three or four items per retrieving turn

stem: A banking assistant's memory pipeline runs nightly over the session store. Customers who state a new preference in the morning ("text me, don't call") and return in the afternoon get the old behavior. Security has rejected memory-writing tools inside the agent, each session transcript averages 15,000 tokens, and running the pipeline over all sessions every hour would be too costly. Run the memory pipeline on demand for a session when it ends, so its durable facts reach the memory store before the customer returns
Run the memory pipeline every hour over all sessions, so that a new preference reaches the memory store within an hour of being stated
Add a memory-writing tool to the agent, so that it saves a new preference to the memory store the moment the customer states it

stem: An operations agent connects to four registered MCPs that expose 120 tools of about 450 tokens each, so every model call starts with 54,000 tokens of definitions. Typical requests use two tools. A regulator requires that eight write tools never be callable by this agent, even if the model asks for them. Remove `get_order_history` from this agent and let it answer archive questions from its general knowledge of earlier orders

stem: A cost-analysis agent nears its window limit after 30 turns. Its history holds five `run_query` results of about 15,000 tokens each. The agent has already reported each result's conclusions to the user, and its final audit summary must cite the query ID of every result it used. stem: A data-platform coding agent's system prompt is 7,500 tokens. It holds four procedures (Delta vacuum policy, job migration steps, cost-tagging workflow, incident write-up template) of about 1,700 tokens each, each used in under 5 percent of requests, plus a 700-token rule that applies to every request: all generated code must use Unity Catalog three-part names. stem: An analytics agent compacts its history at 80 percent of the window using the prompt "Summarize the conversation in five bullet points." stem: A log-triage agent runs 50-step tasks. The team compares two ways to stay within the window on 200 evaluation tasks: a rule that keeps the last 15 messages plus the first user message, and model-based compaction that adds about 4,000 input tokens each time it runs. choices.text: Neither approach; move to a model with a larger window, so that no history ever has to be trimmed or summarized during the tasks
Model-based compaction with a smaller summary, because compaction is the more advanced technique and its cost can be tuned later
Model-based compaction, because it scores one point higher and a summary always keeps more useful information than a fixed rule
The trimming rule, because it meets the 95 percent requirement and avoids the extra model calls that compaction adds

stem: A deployment agent is about to compact its history. The history holds the user's written approval to deploy; a 3,000-line dry-run plan whose resource counts the agent has recorded and the user has approved; the IDs of resources created so far, needed for rollback; five identical `get_status` polling outputs, of which only the latest matters; and an error from a failed step that has not yet been retried. The IDs of the resources created so far, since the agent can list the resources again from the cloud account if needed

stem: A research agent uses conservative compaction that keeps about 70 percent of each history. Traces show a compaction call every three turns, because each summary leaves the history close to the trigger point, and compaction now accounts for 40 percent of token cost. Evaluations show no lost facts. Most of the retained text is raw tool output that is already reflected in the agent's notes. Which adjustment best balances cost and fact retention?

choices.text: Keep conservative compaction but stop it after three passes in a task, letting the history grow freely until the task ends or fails
Compact tool output aggressively while keeping user instructions and the agent's decisions in full, so each pass frees much more space
Switch to aggressive compaction for the whole history, cutting each summary to about 10 percent, including instructions and decisions
Keep conservative compaction and raise the trigger from 80 to 95 percent of the window, so that each compaction call runs a little later

stem: A coordinator dispatches two sub-agents in parallel to handle a customer complaint: one fixes the billing error, and one writes to the customer. Each sub-agent must perform the actions in its own area. Traces show that both opened a support ticket for the same case and both granted a goodwill credit, so the customer received two credits. Give both sub-agents a shared Delta table of actions taken on the case, which each checks and updates before any ticket or credit

stem: A coordinator asks a revenue sub-agent and a margin sub-agent, dispatched minutes apart, to analyze `finance.gold.orders`, a Delta table that a streaming pipeline updates continuously. stem: An orchestrator runs eight research sub-agents, and each returns its findings together with a full log of its tool calls so that auditors can trace every claim. stem: A team runs an interactive data-modeling assistant as a multi-agent system: a coordinator dispatches modeling, naming and documentation sub-agents for each request. stem: A procurement agent runs on a model with a 32,000-token window, and the team reserves 4,000 tokens for output, leaving an input budget of 28,000 tokens. stem: A migration agent writes its discoveries to a notes file that is re-injected into context after every compaction. stem: A contract-analysis agent runs on a model with a 200,000-token window and keeps its full history in context. stem: A claims agent's system prompt v1 is compared in MLflow 3 with v2, which adds a 400-token policy-wording section to every LLM call; both use the same 300-question dataset and judges over three runs each. stem: A team compares three memory configurations for a support agent in MLflow 3, five runs each on the same dataset. stem: A retail assistant persists memories in Lakebase in a table with `user_id`, `kind` (`preference` or `order_note`), `order_id`, `created_at` and `note` columns, and the `note` text is also indexed in AI Search.
